Links: [{"title":"Add Captions to Reels - Auto Subtitles Online","url":"https://flixier.com/tools/auto-subtitle-generator/add-captions-to-reels"},{"title":"How to Add Auto-Captions to Instagram Reels","url":"https://kapwing.com/resources/instagram-reels-captions"},{"title":"How to Add Auto-Captions to Instagram Reels","url":"https://east.kapwing.com/resources/instagram-reels-captions/"},{"title":"Alt Text and Captions on Instagram","url":"https://elgin.edu/accessibility/social-media/instagram/"},{"title":"Instragram Reels Auto-Captions","url":"https://hellosocialize.beehiiv.com/p/instragram-reels-auto-generated-captions"},{"title":"Subscription and credits","url":"https://www.gofaceless.ai/de/tools/instagram-reels-caption-generator"},{"title":"Subscription and credits","url":"https://www.gofaceless.ai/ms/tools/instagram-reels-caption-generator"},{"title":"Subscription and credits","url":"https://www.gofaceless.ai/ar/tools/instagram-reels-caption-generator"},{"title":"Subscription and credits","url":"https://www.gofaceless.ai/zh/tools/instagram-reels-caption-generator"}]

Yes, Instagram can generate auto-captions for Reels in a browser, though the evidence I found is thin. The main source is a university accessibility guide, and the other results focus on the mobile app or third-party tools.

**Browser support:** An Elgin Community College accessibility guide says Instagram will automatically generate captions for reels through both the app and browser. Its browser steps are to open the page where you want to add a caption, open the "Accessibility" dropdown, and switch on the "auto-generated captions" toggle. It notes that the button turns blue to indicate that captions are turned on. I couldn't confirm these steps against Instagram's own help documentation, and web interfaces change often, so the menu names may differ.

**In the app:** Kapwing's guide describes the mobile route. You open the Stickers menu and select the Captions sticker in the Reels editor. Instagram then will automatically transcribe your video and add captions for you. You can also edit the text and style there.

**Editing transcripts:** Kapwing notes that auto-captions tools like Instagram misinterpret a word in cases such as accents, fast speech, background noise, or brand names. Editing is easier on a desktop than on a phone, which is one reason people use third-party tools for transcript cleanup.

**Third-party options:** Several online editors, such as Flixier, offer auto-generated Reel captions in the browser. Flixier says you can upload your Reel, click on Generate Subtitles, and it works without installing software. Export the captions and upload them as your own file if you need to.

If you need a reliable answer, check Instagram's Help Center, since that is the authoritative source on which browser options are currently available.

**Short answer:** Technically feasible, but fragile, and it runs into Instagram's terms of service. Search results didn't surface anything specific about Reels caption markup, so the DOM details below are my general understanding and need testing against the live site.

**Technical feasibility**
- Content scripts are the standard way to do this. They can read the page's DOM and pass what they find to the rest of the extension. They can read details of the web pages the browser visits, make changes to them, and pass information to their parent extension.
- Timing matters. Chrome's default injection point is "document_idle", but Reels is a single-page app that loads more content as you scroll, so a one-time read won't capture it. You'd likely need a MutationObserver or scroll-triggered extraction, plus deduplication by reel ID.
- Expect selectors to break. One write-up notes that traditional DOM scraping is fragile: UI changes, dynamic loading, and anti-bot measures make it unreliable. Class names are often obfuscated and change with deploys, so anchor on stable attributes, such as `aria` labels, `role`, or `href` patterns, and build in fallbacks.
- An alternative is network interception. One tutorial describes injecting a script into the page context to wrap `fetch`/XHR and read the GraphQL responses before they hit the DOM. That can yield structured caption data. But it depends on undocumented internal endpoints, which change without notice, and it's a more aggressive form of the same ToS problem.

**Terms and risk**
- Instagram's terms are the main obstacle. Their terms explicitly forbid automated data collection without prior authorization. The official help center describes data scraping as the automated access and collection of data from a website or app. Unauthorized scraping involves automation to collect information in violation of our Terms of Service.
- Enforcement is real. Accounts can be restricted or flagged, and Instagram has sent cease and desist letters and banned companies from its platform for scraping. Meta has also litigated against scrapers, including a 2024 federal case in which it described its anti-bot defenses.
- Legal status is less settled than ToS status. One source says public content scraping is generally considered legalized in many jurisdictions unless it involves bypassing access or authentication controls. That is a general claim, not legal advice, and it doesn't override contract terms.

**Practical guidance**
- Keep it to what the logged-in user already sees, and avoid bypassing login or authentication.
- Don't scrape at scale. Rate-limit, avoid collecting account or personal data, and don't transmit scraped data to a server.
- If this is for a product or business, check the Chrome Web Store developer policies and consider Meta's official APIs. Those are limited, but they're the sanctioned route.
- If it's personal, a local-only extension that reads visible captions is the lowest-risk version of this idea.

content.text: Instagram and TikTok are not symmetric, and that changes the plan. Let me write this up properly.

cat > "C:/Users/dangi/OneDrive/Desktop/cs124/Project-Fall2026-Dilpickl-67565383/RESEARCH.md" << 'EOF'
# Feasibility research: active fact-checker for short-form video

Date: 2026-10-12. Status: pre-decision. Nothing here is committed yet.

The question that decides the project: **can we get at what a reel actually
says, or only its caption text?** A tool that reads hashtags is a toy. A tool
that reads the spoken claims is real.

## Finding 1: TikTok and Instagram are not symmetric

**TikTok exposes caption tracks, including auto-generated ASR ones, in its
public web player data.** No login, no cookies. Multiple third-party tools do
exactly this today and output WebVTT/SRT. Videos with recognizable speech get
auto-captions; music-only and dance videos legitimately have none.

**Instagram does not.** Its auto-captions are a creator-side authoring feature
(a Captions sticker in the Reels editor), not a public transcript track. The
only route to Instagram transcripts is intercepting internal GraphQL responses
— undocumented, changes without notice, and squarely against their terms. Meta
also enforces this aggressively: cease-and-desists, partner bans, litigation.

**Consequence: build for TikTok first.** Instagram is a stretch goal at best
and possibly should be dropped. This is the single most important finding and
it was not obvious going in.

## Finding 2: "Active" is achievable, but only via caption tracks

If the transcript already exists in the page, there is no transcription step.
That removes the latency wall. TypeSafe judgments return in roughly 150ms, so a
claim-detection pass can finish while the user is still watching the video.

That makes a live badge genuinely feasible — not a promise we have to fake.

Evidence retrieval is the slow part (web search per claim, measured in
seconds). So the design splits:

- **Fast path, automatic:** transcript -> per-sentence judgments -> badge.
  "3 checkable claims" appears during playback.
- **Slow path, on demand:** user taps the badge -> retrieval -> per-source
  stance judgments -> verdicts.

## Finding 3: Audio capture works as a fallback, with real costs

`chrome.tabCapture` plus an MV3 offscreen document can capture tab audio and
feed Whisper. Constraints found:

- Requires a user gesture (extension action click). Cannot run automatically.
- Capturing **mutes the tab** unless the stream is routed back through an
  `AudioContext` to its destination.
- Stream IDs are single-use and expire in seconds.
- Transcription is slow and costs money per minute.

So this is the fallback for videos with no caption track, triggered manually.
Not the primary path.

## Finding 4: Posture matters more than technique

The defensible version is a **local-only extension that reads what the
logged-in user is already looking at**, one video at a time, at human pace,
with nothing shipped to a server beyond the claim text we need to check.

What we will not do: bulk collection, crawling feeds we are not watching,
bypassing authentication, or retaining anyone's data. Those are the things that
draw enforcement and they are also just not necessary for this tool.

content.text:
Wrote it all up in [RESEARCH.md](RESEARCH.md). The headline:

**TikTok and Instagram are not the same problem, and I assumed they were.**

TikTok puts caption tracks — including its auto-generated ASR ones — in its public web player data. No login needed. That means **the transcript already exists in the page.** You don't transcribe anything; you read it.

Instagram doesn't. Its auto-captions are a creator-side editor feature, not a public track. The only way to an Instagram transcript is intercepting internal GraphQL responses, which is undocumented, breaks without warning, and is the exact thing Meta sends cease-and-desists and lawsuits over.

**That one asymmetry resolves your "somehow watches the videos" problem.** Because the transcript is already there, there's no transcription latency — and TypeSafe judgments come back in ~150ms. So a badge saying "3 checkable claims" can genuinely appear *while the video is playing*. That's actually active. Not a fake overlay, not a 30-second spinner.

The design that falls out:

- **Fast and automatic:** content script reads the transcript → TypeSafe fan-out per sentence (is this a checkable claim? what domain? how much harm if wrong?) → badge appears during playback.
- **Slow and on-demand:** user taps the badge → Google's Fact Check API first (cheap, catches already-published checks), then web retrieval, then a supports/contradicts judgment per source → verdict. Low confidence returns "unverified," never a guess.

Two other things worth knowing. Audio capture via `tabCapture` *does* work as a fallback for videos with no captions, but it needs a manual click, it **mutes the tab** unless you route the stream back through an `AudioContext`, and it's slow and costs money per minute — so it's a fallback, not the main path. And the defensible posture here is a local-only extension reading one video the user is already watching, at human pace. No bulk collection, no crawling feeds we aren't watching. That's both the low-risk version and genuinely all you need.

**The decision I'd make, which you should overrule if you disagree: build TikTok-only, and drop Instagram for now.** Instagram roughly doubles the work, adds the only real legal exposure in the project, and is the part most likely to break mid-semester. If TikTok works, Instagram becomes a stretch goal with an honest cost attached.

Now the part that matters more than any of this: **the whole project rests on one unverified assumption** — that those caption tracks are actually readable from a content script on a live TikTok page in 2026. My evidence is strong but indirect: third-party tools do it, but there's no documentation saying it'll keep working.

So I want milestone 1 to be *only* that. Load a TikTok video page, pull the transcript, print it to the console. No judgments, no UI, no fact-checking. If it works, you have a real project. If it doesn't, you find out today instead of in week six, and we pivot while pivoting is still cheap.

Before I build it — **how will you know it worked?** My answer would be: you open a TikTok video you've already watched, and the text the extension prints matches what the person actually said. If you'd call something else the finish line, say it now, because that's what I'll build toward.

Say go and I'll scaffold the extension and we'll test it against a real video.

content.text:
Short answer: **yes on Android, effectively no on iOS** — and which phone you own decides a lot, so that's my question at the end.

**Why iOS is out, independent of the Mac problem.** iOS has no API for reading another app's screen and no way to draw an overlay on top of another app. Safari web extensions only work inside Safari, not the TikTok app. The only hook is a Share Sheet extension. So even with a Mac, passive watching on iPhone isn't a thing Apple permits. You're not missing a trick; the platform forbids it.

**Android genuinely can do this.** Three routes, honestly ranked:

**1. Screen capture + on-device OCR + floating overlay.** `MediaProjection` captures the screen, ML Kit's on-device text recognition (free, fast enough for real-time) reads the caption region, and a `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` bubble draws your badge on top of TikTok. This is how live screen-translation apps work, and it's the real answer to "actively watches." It reads pixels, so it doesn't care about TikTok's internals and won't break when they reshuffle their app.

The catch: OCR only sees text that's *on screen*. Burned-in captions and creator text overlays, yes — and those are everywhere. But a claim that's only spoken aloud with no captions displayed? You get nothing. You also eat a permission prompt and a persistent notification every session, plus battery.

**2. One-tap share target.** Your app registers in TikTok's share sheet. User taps Share → your app → your server resolves the video and pulls the *full* caption track, same as the extension does. One tap, in-flow, not paste. Reliable and deep — it gets everything the person said, not just what's on screen. But the user has to initiate it per video.

**3. Accessibility Service.** Can read on-screen text nodes from other apps. Problem: video content is a rendered surface, so burned-in captions are pixels, not nodes — and it's unclear how much of TikTok's UI exposes real text. Google Play also restricts accessibility APIs to actual accessibility use and removes apps that abuse them. Sideloading for a class project sidesteps the policy, but the technical uncertainty alone makes this the worst of the three.

So the real mobile tradeoff is **passive but shallow (OCR) vs. one tap but complete (share)**. My instinct is you'd want both: the bubble watches passively and flags on-screen claims, and a "check this properly" action pulls the full transcript.

**Here's the part that makes this cheap, though.** The extension already needs a server-side endpoint, because the TypeSafe key can't ship in client code. Which means the interesting half of this project — claim detection, retrieval, stance judgment, verdict composition — lives in one HTTP endpoint from day one, regardless of platform. An Android app then isn't a rewrite. It's a second thin client calling the same endpoint. Mobile costs you Kotlin and an overlay, not a second brain.

So the order I'd recommend: **Chrome extension first, because it's the fastest way to prove the pipeline works against real TikTok data. Then Android as a second client.** Not because mobile matters less — you're right that it's where reels actually get watched — but because debugging claim detection is much easier when you're not also fighting MediaProjection permissions and OCR noise. The hard thinking transfers; the plumbing doesn't need to be solved twice.

I'll put mobile in `PLAN.md` as a committed goal rather than a maybe, so it shapes the backend from the start.

**What phone do you have?** If it's Android, mobile is real and we build toward it. If it's an iPhone, then an Android app only ever runs on an emulator on your laptop — which still satisfies the class requirement, but you'd never actually use the thing yourself, and that changes whether it's worth your hours.

content.text:
Right instinct — let me show you instead of describing it. But first, the design decisions that matter, because they're the ones that'll make or break whether anyone keeps this installed.

**The badge must never imply "false" before you've checked anything.** Detecting a claim and judging a claim are two different operations, separated by seconds. If the badge turns red the moment it finds a sentence with a number in it, you've built a tool that cries wolf on true statements. So detection is neutral-colored and says *"3 checkable claims"* — not a verdict.

**Quiet by default.** Most reels have nothing checkable. If a widget pops up on every video, it gets uninstalled by Thursday. No claims means no UI, or near enough.

**Per-claim, not per-video.** A reel can contain one accurate claim and one false one. A single "trust score" for a video would be dishonest, and it's the thing every existing tool gets wrong.

**"Unverified" is a real answer, visually distinct from "false."** Honestly, a lot of novel claims will land there, and pretending otherwise is how you lose credibility.

Let me render it.

# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-voice)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - **Fullscreen / expand buttons**: there is no fullscreen. Never call any element's `requestFullscreen()`, never call `document.exitFullscreen()`, and never key state on `document.fullscreenElement` (the API is dead inside the widget iframe and `fullscreenElement` stays null forever, so a label or branch keyed on it is permanently stuck), never call display-mode host APIs, and never fake fullscreen by restyling your container to viewport size — all of these produce dead or broken controls on at least one platform. If the user asks for a fullscreen or expand button, implement an expanded-layout toggle instead: a synchronous CSS class flip on in-flow content with explicit px sizes (taller chart, roomier controls), updating the button label in the same handler — no async, no awaits, symmetric enter/exit. Mutate the existing elements' classes and text; never rebuild the control's DOM with innerHTML (replacement silently drops event listeners and leaves a dead button). The host resizes to fit your content automatically. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--radius)` for controls, `12px` for cards. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. Tokens tell you _what_ you can use; the [Rules](../CLAUDE.md#rules) tell you _how_ to apply them. These principles tell you _why_. ## Claude-native cds is designed to be authored _by_ Claude as much as _for_ Claude's products. The `CLAUDE.md` you're reading is the system prompt; component docs are structured for retrieval; utilities are named so a model can guess them; the GenerateDemo page proves the loop works. A design system an LLM can use fluently is one humans can use fluently too. ## Clay is Claude's color `brand` (clay) is reserved for what Claude does — send, generate, the spark mark. User-driven primary actions take the neutral `accent` blue; everything else stays gray. Holding clay back to a single role is what lets it carry meaning instead of becoming wallpaper. ## Serif is Claude's voice Claude's responses render in serif; the surrounding chrome stays sans. Typography signals who's speaking before a word is read. cds ships `--font-voice` (the `font-voice` utility) for response surfaces. ## Density adapts to the surface Console, claude.ai and antfarm share the same components — `compact` for dev tools and power users, `comfortable` for consumer apps. Density is one switch on `CdsRoot`, not a per-component prop, so a product can change its feel without forking a single component. ## Built to be composed, not overridden Every component takes `className` for placement and behavior, every token is a public CSS var, and compound parts (`.Root`, `.Item`, `.Trigger`) sit under the porcelain helpers so you can recombine them. The system expects you to compose _with_ it — wrap it, arrange it, fill its slots, build new things from its tokens — not restyle it from outside or fork it. When props and parts can't reach what you need, the system is missing something: the fix goes into cds (see the [`className` rule](../CLAUDE.md#classname-rule)), not around it. ## Restraint over options One accent per view, one elevation step, t-shirt sizes instead of 0–12 scales. Fewer decisions at the call site means fewer ways for two screens to drift apart — consistency comes from removing knobs, not policing them. ## CDS tokens Every visual decision in `@ant/cds` resolves to a `--*` CSS custom property. Pair with `--text-tint-{hue}` (utility `text-tint-{hue}`; hue-600, 300 in dark) so bg and text follow the same CdsRoot's mode. `--bg-tint-{hue}-opaque` (utility `bg-tint-{hue}-opaque`) is that opaque stop as a token; a surface scope whose backdrop is a fill rather than a plane (CoachMark's accent card, `surface="fill-accent"`) re-points each `--bg-tint-{hue}` at it inline, because the un-mix only holds over a plane. The tints are solved against the stock `surface-1`, so a theme that overrides `--surface-*` should override `--bg-tint-*` in the same block if it needs the exact stops, and `--bg-tint-*-opaque` with them: inside a fill scope the inline pin reads the opaque token, not the tint. #### `git-*` roles Diff and PR/CR-state colors — `added`, `removed`, `modified`, `conflicting`, `merged`, `closed`, `draft`, plus `opened`/`queued` as aliases of `added`/`modified`. Each carries the full `text` / `fill{,-hover}` / `bg` / `border` / `on` suite. Values are hues matching the palette claude.ai's diff UI was built on (not CDS ramp stops), so adopting them there is a pure rename; `fill` light is the hue darkened just enough for white `on-git-*` to pass AA. ### Background vs. fill Both are backgrounds; the split is saturation, and therefore which foreground token pairs on top. `bg-{role}` is the pale tint (hue-100 light / hue-800 dark) for passive status surfaces — Banner, chip; Badge paints its translucent twin `bg-tint-{hue}`. Light enough that `text-{role}` (hue-600) reads against it: a danger banner is `bg-danger` + `text-danger`. `fill-{role}` is the saturated solid (hue-450) for interactive controls — button, checkbox, toggle. Too dark for `text-{role}`, so it pairs with `on-{role}` (gray-0 / gray-900) instead; the 450 stop is chosen for WCAG contrast against `on-*`. | | Background | Foreground | Example | | ----- | ------------- | ------------- | ------------- | | Tint | `bg-{role}` | `text-{role}` | Banner, Toast | | Solid | `fill-{role}` | `on-{role}` | Button | The token name encodes the pairing: use `bg-*` when the hue is ambient context behind body text; `fill-*` when the hue _is_ the control surface. ### Purpose tokens | Token | Value (light) | Use case | | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | | `--text-primary` | `neutral-900` | Body text | | `--text-secondary` | `neutral-600` | Supporting text | | `--text-muted` | `neutral-400` | Placeholder, captions | | `--text-disabled` | `alpha-4` | Disabled labels | | `--border` | `alpha-2` | Default 1px hairline | | `--border-strong` | `alpha-3` | Emphasized divider | | `--border-stronger` | `neutral-900 / 40%` | Heavy divider | | `--fill-primary` | `neutral-900` | Primary button bg | | `--fill-primary-hover` | `neutral-750` | | | `--fill-secondary` | `hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.1)` | Secondary button bg | | `--fill-secondary-hover` | `alpha-1` | | | `--fill-secondary-ring` | `border` (light) / transparent (dark) | Secondary button ring | | `--fill-field` | `hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.5)` (light) / `alpha-1` (dark) | Field control bg (TextInput, TextArea, Combobox) | | `--fill-field-ring` | `border` (light + dark) | Field control resting ring | | `--fill-ghost-hover` | `alpha-1` (light) / 7.5% white (dark half-step) | Ghost button / row hover bg | | `--fill-ghost-selected` | `alpha-2` (light) / 15% white (dark half-step) | Ghost row / nav item selected bg | | `--fill-control` | `alpha-2` | Avatar fallback bg | | `--fill-control-hover` | `alpha-3` | | | `--fill-disabled` | `alpha-1` | Disabled control bg | | `--on-primary` | `neutral-0` | Text on `fill-primary` | | `--on-accent` | `gray-0` | Text on `accent` | | `--on-brand` | `#ffffff` | Text on `brand` | | `--on-danger` | `gray-0` | Text on `danger` | | `--on-success` | `gray-900` | Text on `success` | | `--on-warning` | `gray-900` | Text on `warning` | | `--on-pro` | `gray-0` | Text on `pro` | | `--focus-shadow` | `0 0 0 1px accent, 0 0 6px 1px bg-accent` | `focus-visible` ring | | `--shadow-sm` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Low elevation | | `--shadow-md` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Card / panel | | `--shadow-lg` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Dialog / sheet | | `--shadow-popover` | `0 8px 24px /12%, 0 2px 6px /8%` | Menu, dropdown popups | | `--surface-popover` | `surface-3` | Named alias | | `--surface-panel` | `surface-2` | Named alias | `--shadow-sm/md/lg` are two-layer composites (contact + diffused drop) driven by `--shadow-color`, which deepens to `black/24%` in dark mode. `--shadow-popover` is a fixed two-layer literal tuned for floating menus. --- ## CDS content How to write the words that go inside cds components. Tokens decide how the UI _looks_; this decides how it _sounds_. The voice is **intelligent, warm, unvarnished, and collaborative** — your smartest friend explaining something in plain terms. Friendly lives in the copy, not in extra chrome. ## Mechanics - **Sentence case everywhere.** Buttons, headings, tabs, labels, menu items. "Save changes", not "Save Changes". Title Case is for proper nouns only (Claude, Opus, Anthropic Console). - **No terminal punctuation on labels and headings.** Helper text, descriptions, and empty-state body copy _do_ end with a period. - **Use contractions.** "Can't", "you'll", "it's". Conversational, not stiff. - **Active voice, verb first.** "Delete project", not "Project deletion". - **Ellipsis = in progress only.** "Claude is thinking…". Not for trailing off, not for menu suffixes. - **No ampersands.** Spell out "and". - **Serial comma.** "Chats, projects, and artifacts." ## Pronouns UI speaks as the product, not as Claude and not as the user. | Context | Use | Example | | ---------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | User's things | **your** | "Your projects" — never "My projects" | | Confirmations | none / past tense | "Saved", "Got it" — never "I saved it" | | Errors | **you / your** | "Your session expired" — never "I couldn't…" | | Claude (in chat) | **I** | Reserved for the chat surface; system UI never says "I" | ## Words to avoid | Skip | Why | Instead | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------- | | "successfully" | The success toast _is_ the success | "File uploaded" | | "please" | UI isn't asking a favor | "Enter a name" | | "Click here" / "Tap to…" | Link text should name the destination | "Read the docs" | | "!" on system copy | Reads as shouty | "Settings saved" | | "leverage", "seamless", "unlock", "empower" | Corporate filler | Say what it does | | "simply", "just", "easy" | Presumes — and condescends | Cut it | ## Patterns **Buttons / CTAs** — verb first, 1–3 words, sentence case, no punctuation. "Create project", "Upgrade to Pro". Not "OK", "Submit", or "Click to continue". **Errors** — say what happened, then what to do. One sentence, no "Error:" prefix, no first person. "That name's already taken. Try another." Never surface raw exception strings. **Empty states** — an invitation, not an apology. Headline names the space ("Start your first project"), one-line body explains it, CTA is a verb ("Create project"). Skip "Nothing here yet." **Placeholders** — a real example of valid input ("name@company.com", "Summarize this document"). No "e.g." prefix, don't repeat the field label. **Links** — describe where they go ("Learn more", "View pricing"). Keep them at the end of the sentence; punctuation sits outside the link. ## Do / Don't | Do | Don't | | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | | "File uploaded" | "Your file was uploaded successfully!" | | "Enter a workspace name" | "Please enter a workspace name." | | "Couldn't connect to Slack. Retry" | "Error: I was unable to connect." | | "Your projects" | "My projects" | | "Create project" | "Click Here To Get Started" | | "Connect Slack" | "Add the Slack Connector" | Do not overthink. Try to keep thinking below 500 tokens. If the visual is complex and requires more reasoning effort, consider creating an artifact instead.

# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-voice)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - **Fullscreen / expand buttons**: there is no fullscreen. Never call any element's `requestFullscreen()`, never call `document.exitFullscreen()`, and never key state on `document.fullscreenElement` (the API is dead inside the widget iframe and `fullscreenElement` stays null forever, so a label or branch keyed on it is permanently stuck), never call display-mode host APIs, and never fake fullscreen by restyling your container to viewport size — all of these produce dead or broken controls on at least one platform. If the user asks for a fullscreen or expand button, implement an expanded-layout toggle instead: a synchronous CSS class flip on in-flow content with explicit px sizes (taller chart, roomier controls), updating the button label in the same handler — no async, no awaits, symmetric enter/exit. Mutate the existing elements' classes and text; never rebuild the control's DOM with innerHTML (replacement silently drops event listeners and leaves a dead button). The host resizes to fit your content automatically. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--radius)` for controls, `12px` for cards. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - **Validate input in interactive widgets.** Any widget that collects user input before acting on it (quiz answers, text boxes, form fields) must check that input in its submit handler: if a required field is empty or invalid, show a clear inline error next to the control (13px `color: var(--text-danger)` text, e.g. "Enter an answer first") and stop — do not advance to the next step, reveal the answer, or otherwise proceed until the input is valid. Clear the error as soon as the user edits the field. - Scripts execute after streaming — load libraries via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` (UMD globals), then use the global in a plain `<script>` that follows. The library `<script src>` tag must come BEFORE any inline script that uses its global — never call a library from code that appears above its `<script src>` tag. - **CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external resources may ONLY load from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`, `fonts.googleapis.com`, `fonts.gstatic.com`. All other origins are blocked by the sandbox — the request silently fails. ### CSS Variables **Surfaces**: `--surface-2` (white), `--surface-1` (card), `--surface-0` (page bg); role tints `--bg-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Text**: `--text-primary` (black), `--text-secondary` (muted), `--text-muted` (hints); role `--text-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Borders**: `--border` (default hairline), `--border-strong` (hover), `--border-stronger`; role `--border-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Typography**: `--font-sans`, `--font-voice` (serif), `--font-mono` **Layout**: `--radius` (8px), `--pad-{sm,md,lg,xl}`, `--gap-{xs,sm,md,lg,xl}`; for larger corners use literal `12px`/`16px` All auto-adapt to light/dark mode. For custom colors in HTML, use CSS variables. **Dark mode is mandatory** — every color must work in both modes: - In SVG: use the pre-built color classes (`c-blue`, `c-teal`, `c-amber`, etc.) for colored nodes — they handle light/dark mode automatically. Never write `<style>` blocks for colors. - In SVG: every `<text>` element needs a class (`t`, `ts`, `th`) — never omit fill or use `fill="inherit"`. Inside a `c-{color}` parent, text classes auto-adjust to the ramp. - In HTML: always use CSS variables (--text-primary, --text-secondary) for text. Never hardcode colors like color: #333 — invisible in dark mode. - Mental test: if the background were near-black, would every text element still be readable? ### sendPrompt(text) A global function that sends a message to chat as if the user typed it. Use it when the user's next step benefits from Claude thinking. Handle filtering, sorting, toggling, and calculations in JS instead. ### Links `<a href="https://...">` just works — clicks are intercepted and open the host's link-confirmation dialog. Or call `openLink(url)` directly. ## When nothing fits Pick the closest use case below and adapt. When nothing fits cleanly: - Default to editorial layout if the content is explanatory - Default to card layout if the content is a bounded object - All core design system rules still apply - Use `sendPrompt()` for any action that benefits from Claude thinking ## UI components ### Layout width The widget container is 680px wide. Use `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(160px, 1fr))` for responsive columns — auto-fit lets the grid pick column count by available width. ### Aesthetic Flat, clean, white surfaces. Minimal 0.5px borders. Generous whitespace. No gradients, no shadows (except functional focus rings). Everything should feel native to claude.ai — like it belongs on the page, not embedded from somewhere else. ### Tokens - Borders: always `0.5px solid var(--border)` (or `--border-strong` for emphasis) - Corner radius: `var(--radius)` for most elements, `12px` for cards - Cards: white bg (`var(--surface-2)`), 0.5px border, 12px radius, padding 1rem 1.25rem - Form elements (input, select, textarea, button, range slider) are pre-styled — write bare tags. Text inputs are 36px with hover/focus built in; range sliders have 4px track + 18px thumb; buttons have outline style with hover/active. Only add inline styles to override (e.g., different width). - Buttons: pre-styled with transparent bg, 0.5px `--border-strong` border, hover `--surface-1`, active scale(0.98). If it triggers sendPrompt, append a ↗ arrow. - **Round every displayed number.** JS float math leaks artifacts — `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`, `7 * 1.1` gives `7.700000000000001`. Any number that reaches the screen (slider readouts, stat card values, axis labels, data-point labels, tooltips, computed totals) must go through `Math.round()`, `.toFixed(n)`, or `Intl.NumberFormat`. Pick the precision that makes sense for the context — integers for counts, 1–2 decimals for percentages, `toLocaleString()` for currency. For range sliders, also set `step="1"` (or step="0.1" etc.) so the input itself emits round values. - Spacing: use rem for vertical rhythm (1rem, 1.5rem, 2rem), px for component-internal gaps (8px, 12px, 16px) - Box-shadows: none, except `box-shadow: 0 0 0 Npx` focus rings on inputs ### Metric cards For summary numbers (revenue, count, percentage) — surface card with muted 13px label above, 24px/500 number below. `background: var(--surface-1)`, no border, `border-radius: var(--radius)`, padding 1rem. Use in grids of 2-4 with `gap: 12px`. Distinct from raised cards (which have white bg + border). ### Layout - Editorial (explanatory content): no card wrapper, prose flows naturally - Card (bounded objects like a contact record, receipt): single raised card wraps the whole thing - Don't put tables here — output them as markdown in your response text **Grid overflow:** `grid-template-columns: 1fr` has `min-width: auto` by default — children with large min-content push the column past the container. Use `minmax(0, 1fr)` to clamp. **Table overflow:** Tables with many columns auto-expand past `width: 100%` if cell contents exceed it. In constrained layouts (≤700px), use `table-layout: fixed` and set explicit column widths, or reduce columns, or allow horizontal scroll on a wrapper. ### Mockup presentation Contained mockups — mobile screens, chat threads, single cards, modals, small UI components — should sit on a background surface (`var(--surface-1)` container with `border-radius: 12px` and padding, or a device frame) so they don't float naked on the widget canvas. Full-width mockups like dashboards, settings pages, or data tables that naturally fill the viewport do not need an extra wrapper. ### 1. Interactive explainer — learn how something works *"Explain how compound interest works" / "Teach me about sorting algorithms"* Use HTML for the interactive controls — sliders, buttons, live state displays, charts. Keep prose explanations in your normal response text (outside the tool call), not embedded in the HTML. No card wrapper. Whitespace is the container. ```html <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <label style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-secondary);">Years</label> <input type="range" min="1" max="40" value="20" id="years" style="flex: 1;" /> <span style="font-size: 14px; font-weight: 500; min-width: 24px;" id="years-out">20</span> </div> <div style="display: flex; align-items: baseline; gap: 8px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <span style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-secondary);">£1,000 →</span> <span style="font-size: 24px; font-weight: 500;" id="result">£3,870</span> </div> <div style="margin: 2rem 0; position: relative; height: 240px;"> <canvas id="chart"></canvas> </div> ``` Use `sendPrompt()` to let users ask follow-ups: `sendPrompt('What if I increase the rate to 10%?')` ### 2. Compare options — decision making *"Compare pricing and features of these products" / "Help me choose between React and Vue"* Use HTML. Side-by-side card grid for options. Highlight differences with semantic colors. Interactive elements for filtering or weighting. - Each option in a card. Use badges for key differentiators. A leading Tabler icon (`<i class="ti ti-NAME">` at 20px, `aria-hidden`) anchors each option visually — pick the most apt name per option. - Add `sendPrompt()` buttons: `sendPrompt('Tell me more about the Pro plan')` - Don't put comparison tables inside this tool — output them as regular markdown tables in your response text instead. The tool is for the visual card grid only. - When one option is recommended or "most popular", accent its card with `border: 2px solid var(--border-accent)` only (2px is deliberate — the only exception to the 0.5px rule, used to accent featured items) — keep the same background and border as the other cards. Add a small badge (e.g. "Most popular") above or inside the card header using `background: var(--bg-accent); color: var(--text-accent); font-size: 12px; padding: 4px 12px; border-radius: var(--radius)`. ### 3. Data record — bounded UI object *"Show me a Salesforce contact card" / "Create a receipt for this order"* Use HTML. Wrap the entire thing in a single raised card. All content is sans-serif since it's pure UI. Use an avatar/initials circle for people (see example below). ```html <div style="background: var(--surface-2); border-radius: 12px; border: 0.5px solid var(--border); padding: 1rem 1.25rem;"> <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 16px;"> <div style="width: 44px; height: 44px; border-radius: 50%; background: var(--bg-accent); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; font-weight: 500; font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-accent);">MR</div> <div> <p style="font-weight: 500; font-size: 15px; margin: 0;">Maya Rodriguez</p> <p style="font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0;">VP of Engineering</p> </div> </div> <div style="border-top: 0.5px solid var(--border); padding-top: 12px;"> <table style="width: 100%; font-size: 13px;"> <tr><td style="color: var(--text-secondary); padding: 4px 0;"><i class="ti ti-mail" style="font-size:16px; vertical-align:-2px; margin-right:6px" aria-hidden="true"></i>Email</td><td style="text-align: right; padding: 4px 0; color: var(--text-accent);">m.rodriguez@acme.com</td></tr> <tr><td style="color: var(--text-secondary); padding: 4px 0;"><i class="ti ti-phone" style="font-size:16px; vertical-align:-2px; margin-right:6px" aria-hidden="true"></i>Phone</td><td style="text-align: right; padding: 4px 0;">+1 (415) 555-0172</td></tr> </table> </div> </div> ``` ## Color palette 9 color ramps, each with 7 stops from lightest to darkest. 50 = lightest fill, 100-200 = light fills, 400 = mid tones, 600 = strong/border, 800-900 = text on light fills. | Class | Ramp | 50 (lightest) | 100 | 200 | 400 | 600 | 800 | 900 (darkest) | |-------|------|------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|------| | `c-purple` | Purple | #EEEDFE | #CECBF6 | #AFA9EC | #7F77DD | #534AB7 | #3C3489 | #26215C | | `c-teal` | Teal | #E1F5EE | #9FE1CB | #5DCAA5 | #1D9E75 | #0F6E56 | #085041 | #04342C | | `c-coral` | Coral | #FAECE7 | #F5C4B3 | #F0997B | #D85A30 | #993C1D | #712B13 | #4A1B0C | | `c-pink` | Pink | #FBEAF0 | #F4C0D1 | #ED93B1 | #D4537E | #993556 | #72243E | #4B1528 | | `c-gray` | Gray | #F1EFE8 | #D3D1C7 | #B4B2A9 | #888780 | #5F5E5A | #444441 | #2C2C2A | | `c-blue` | Blue | #E6F1FB | #B5D4F4 | #85B7EB | #378ADD | #185FA5 | #0C447C | #042C53 | | `c-green` | Green | #EAF3DE | #C0DD97 | #97C459 | #639922 | #3B6D11 | #27500A | #173404 | | `c-amber` | Amber | #FAEEDA | #FAC775 | #EF9F27 | #BA7517 | #854F0B | #633806 | #412402 | | `c-red` | Red | #FCEBEB | #F7C1C1 | #F09595 | #E24B4A | #A32D2D | #791F1F | #501313 | **How to assign colors**: Color should encode meaning, not sequence. Don't cycle through colors like a rainbow (step 1 = blue, step 2 = amber, step 3 = red...). Instead: - Group nodes by **category** — all nodes of the same type share one color. E.g. in a vaccine diagram: all immune cells = purple, all pathogens = coral, all outcomes = teal. - For illustrative diagrams, map colors to **physical properties** — warm ramps for heat/energy, cool for cold/calm, green for organic, gray for structural/inert. - Use **gray for neutral/structural** nodes (start, end, generic steps). - Use **2-3 colors per diagram**, not 6+. More colors = more visual noise. A diagram with gray + purple + teal is cleaner than one using every ramp. - **Prefer purple, teal, coral, pink** for general diagram categories. Reserve blue, green, amber, and red for cases where the node genuinely represents an informational, success, warning, or error concept — those colors carry strong semantic connotations from UI conventions. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use blue/amber/red freely when they map to physical properties like temperature or pressure.) **Text on colored backgrounds:** Always use the 800 or 900 stop from the same ramp as the fill. Never use black, gray, or --text-primary on colored fills. **When a box has both a title and a subtitle, they must be two different stops** — title darker (800 in light mode, 100 in dark), subtitle lighter (600 in light, 200 in dark). Same stop for both reads flat; the weight difference alone isn't enough. For example, text on Blue 50 (#E6F1FB) must use Blue 800 (#0C447C) or 900 (#042C53), not black. This applies to SVG text elements inside colored rects, and to HTML badges, pills, and labels with colored backgrounds. **Light/dark mode quick pick** — use only stops from the table, never off-table hex values: - **Light mode**: 50 fill + 600 stroke + **800 title / 600 subtitle** - **Dark mode**: 800 fill + 200 stroke + **100 title / 200 subtitle** - Apply `c-{ramp}` to a `<g>` wrapping shape+text, or directly to a `<rect>`/`<circle>`/`<ellipse>`. Never to `<path>` — paths don't get ramp fill. For colored connector strokes use inline `stroke="#..."` (any mid-ramp hex works in both modes). Dark mode is automatic for ramp classes. Available: c-gray, c-blue, c-red, c-amber, c-green, c-teal, c-purple, c-coral, c-pink. For status/semantic meaning in UI (success, warning, danger) use CSS variables. For categorical coloring in both diagrams and UI, use these ramps. <!-- @generated by apps/cds-docs/scripts/gen-cds-skill.mjs from packages/cds/{CLAUDE.md,docs/**}. Keep them enabled and respond on use (disabled controls are low-contrast and show no tooltip on touch); use `disabledReason` only when you genuinely must disable. - Dense lists: bordered rows, not rounded-rect cards. ### Elevation rule `surface-0` is the page canvas (via `--page-bg`; set it with `CdsRoot`'s `pageBackground` prop); `1`/`2`/`3` step above it. At most **two** floating elevations (`panel` / `popover`) on screen at once. A third floating layer means `Dialog`, not popover-on-popover. Flat in-flow tiles (`rounded-card bg-surface-1 shadow-card-ring`) have no depth and don't count toward this limit. --- ## CDS principles How something feels like Claude — the philosophy behind the tokens. Tokens tell you _what_ you can use; the [Rules](../CLAUDE.md#rules) tell you _how_ to apply them. These principles tell you _why_. ## Claude-native cds is designed to be authored _by_ Claude as much as _for_ Claude's products. The `CLAUDE.md` you're reading is the system prompt; component docs are structured for retrieval; utilities are named so a model can guess them; the GenerateDemo page proves the loop works. A design system an LLM can use fluently is one humans can use fluently too. ## Clay is Claude's color `brand` (clay) is reserved for what Claude does — send, generate, the spark mark. User-driven primary actions take the neutral `accent` blue; everything else stays gray. Holding clay back to a single role is what lets it carry meaning instead of becoming wallpaper. ## Serif is Claude's voice Claude's responses render in serif; the surrounding chrome stays sans. Typography signals who's speaking before a word is read. cds ships `--font-voice` (the `font-voice` utility) for response surfaces. ## Density adapts to the surface Console, claude.ai and antfarm share the same components — `compact` for dev tools and power users, `comfortable` for consumer apps. Density is one switch on `CdsRoot`, not a per-component prop, so a product can change its feel without forking a single component. ## Built to be composed, not overridden Every component takes `className` for placement and behavior, every token is a public CSS var, and compound parts (`.Root`, `.Item`, `.Trigger`) sit under the porcelain helpers so you can recombine them. The system expects you to compose _with_ it — wrap it, arrange it, fill its slots, build new things from its tokens — not restyle it from outside or fork it. When props and parts can't reach what you need, the system is missing something: the fix goes into cds (see the [`className` rule](../CLAUDE.md#classname-rule)), not around it. ## Restraint over options One accent per view, one elevation step, t-shirt sizes instead of 0–12 scales. Fewer decisions at the call site means fewer ways for two screens to drift apart — consistency comes from removing knobs, not policing them. ## CDS tokens Every visual decision in `@ant/cds` resolves to a `--*` CSS custom property. The TypeScript source of truth lives under `packages/cds/tokens/`; `yarn gen:tokens` emits the shipped CSS at [`src/generated/tokens.css`](../src/generated/tokens.css). Tokens are layered so that a single edit at the bottom (a hex value) propagates through ramps, roles, and purposes without touching component code. ## The layer model ``` 1. Base palette --{hue}-{stop} literal hex, mode-stable (gray, red, orange, yellow, green, aqua, blue, violet, magenta) 2. Theme ramps --neutral-N gray-N in light, gray-(900-N) in dark --alpha-N neutral-900 @ fixed opacity (so it flips too) 3. Elevation --surface-{0..3} 0 = darkest, 3 = lightest, in BOTH modes 4. Purpose --surface-{popover, what components actually consume; includes the panel}, --text-*, role mappings ({fill|bg|border|text}-{role}) --fill-*, --on-* — page-bg --page-bg hook the host app sets to its canvas color 5. Density --h-control*, rem lengths (px ÷ 16); remapped by --pad-*, --gap-*, [data-density] --radius, --font-size-*, --leading-* 6. Motion --dur-*, durations + easing curves (mode/density-invariant) --ease-* ``` **Components only read layer 4 (and 5 for sizing).** Layers 1–3 are wiring. --- ## 1. Base palette Literal hex values, mode-stable — `gray-500` is the same pixel in light and dark. The ramp variables resolve anywhere in the document, not only under a `.cds-root`. Nine hues share one 36-stop grid (0, 10–100 by 10, 150–800 by 50, 810–900 by 10); every hue anchors 0 = `#ffffff` and 900 = `#0b0b0b`. Theme ramps `--neutral-N` is `gray-N` in light and `gray-(900-N)` in dark, so `neutral-0` is always the near-background end and `neutral-900` the near-foreground end. Use it for "contrast against the page" (text, borders, fills); use `gray-*` when you mean a specific pixel value regardless of mode. `--alpha-N` is `neutral-900` at fixed opacity — a black wash in light, a white wash in dark, without per-mode overrides. --- ## 3. Elevation | Token | Light | Dark | Use case | | ----------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------ | | `--surface-0` | `gray-20` | `gray-900` | Page | | `--surface-1` | `gray-10` | `gray-850` | In-flow card | | `--surface-2` | `gray-0` | `gray-830` | Panel | | `--surface-3` | `gray-0` | `gray-800` | Popover | The ordinal is absolute lightness in both modes: 0 is the darkest, 3 the lightest. `--surface-panel` and `--surface-popover` alias levels 2 and 3. Purpose **This is the layer components consume.** ### Roles Each role maps a semantic meaning to a hue. Property-first pattern: `--fill-{role}` (solid hue-450), `--fill-{role}-hover` (hue-400), `--bg-{role}` (hue-100 / dark hue-800), `--border-{role}` (solid hue-250 in light / hue-700 in dark), `--text-{role}` (600 fg). Warning's fill diverges: yellow-200 / hover yellow-250. Brand uses named `clay-emphasized` / hover `clay` (not hue stops). The five hue-backed roles reach their hue through internal aliases (`--role-{role}-{stop}`, plus `--role-{role}-fill`, `--role-{role}-fill-hover` and `--role-{role}-on`): CSS-only wiring, not part of the token vocabulary, so never reference them. Charts, palette tints and the `{hue}-{stop}` utilities read the hue ramps directly. | Role | Hue | Tokens | | --------- | ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `accent` | blue | `--fill-accent{,-hover}`, `--bg-accent`, `--bg-accent-muted`, `--border-accent`, `--text-accent` | | `brand` | clay | `--fill-brand{,-hover}`, `--on-brand` (fill-only — no text/bg/border) | | `danger` | red | `--fill-danger{,-hover}`, `--bg-danger`, `--border-danger`, `--text-danger` | | `success` | green | `--fill-success{,-hover}`, `--bg-success`, `--border-success`, `--text-success` | | `warning` | yellow | `--fill-warning{,-hover}`, `--bg-warning`, `--border-warning`, `--text-warning` | | `pro` | purple | `--fill-pro{,-hover}`, `--bg-pro`, `--border-pro`, `--text-pro` | `accent` additionally carries `--bg-accent-muted` (a 10% `fill-accent` wash over transparent, `color-mix` in srgb): an accent wash one weight below `bg-accent`, for tinted-but-quiet accent surfaces — like a reacted reaction pill — where `bg-accent`'s solid hue-100/800 reads too heavy. `--bg-highlight` is built the same way from `warning`'s fill (a 33% `fill-warning` wash over transparent): the highlighter tint behind marked text — search-match substrings, prose `<mark>`. Tokens decide how the UI _looks_; this decides how it _sounds_. The voice is **intelligent, warm, unvarnished, and collaborative** — your smartest friend explaining something in plain terms. Friendly lives in the copy, not in extra chrome. ## Mechanics - **Sentence case everywhere.** Buttons, headings, tabs, labels, menu items. "Save changes", not "Save Changes". Title Case is for proper nouns only (Claude, Opus, Anthropic Console). - **No terminal punctuation on labels and headings.** Helper text, descriptions, and empty-state body copy _do_ end with a period. - **Use contractions.** "Can't", "you'll", "it's". Conversational, not stiff. - **Active voice, verb first.** "Delete project", not "Project deletion". - **Ellipsis = in progress only.** "Claude is thinking…". Not for trailing off, not for menu suffixes. - **No ampersands.** Spell out "and". - **Serial comma.** "Chats, projects, and artifacts." ## Pronouns UI speaks as the product, not as Claude and not as the user. | Context | Use | Example | | ---------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | User's things | **your** | "Your projects" — never "My projects" | | Confirmations | none / past tense | "Saved", "Got it" — never "I saved it" | | Errors | **you / your** | "Your session expired" — never "I couldn't…" | | Claude (in chat) | **I** | Reserved for the chat surface; system UI never says "I" | ## Words to avoid | Skip | Why | Instead | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------- | | "successfully" | The success toast _is_ the success | "File uploaded" | | "please" | UI isn't asking a favor | "Enter a name" | | "Click here" / "Tap to…" | Link text should name the destination | "Read the docs" | | "!" on system copy | Reads as shouty | "Settings saved" | | "leverage", "seamless", "unlock", "empower" | Corporate filler | Say what it does | | "simply", "just", "easy" | Presumes — and condescends | Cut it | ## Patterns **Buttons / CTAs** — verb first, 1–3 words, sentence case, no punctuation. content.text:
Click through the five buttons above the mockup. It opens on state 3 because that's the one where the design matters most.

How it plays out as you scroll:

1. **Scanning.** The extension reads the transcript from the page and judges every sentence at once. That takes about 150 ms, so you'd barely see this state.
2. **Nothing checkable.** Most videos end up here. A faint "Nothing to check" shows for a second and fades, and no panel opens.
3. **Claims found.** The badge turns blue and counts the claims, still with no verdict. The panel lists each claim with its topic and says plainly that nothing has been judged yet. You click **Check these** to start the slow part.
4. **Verdicts.** Every claim gets its own result and source count. The badge only turns red once a claim has actually been contradicted.
5. **No transcript.** Shown for music or dance videos with no speech. It offers to listen to the tab's audio and tells you up front what that costs.

A few choices I made that you didn't ask for, so you can overrule them:

- **I added a fourth verdict, "Misleading."** "The FDA has never tested it" shows why: it can be technically true and still give the wrong impression. Supported / contradicted / unverified can't express that. It also makes the judging harder, so we could leave it out of the first version.
- **The badge sits in the top-left of the video**, where it doesn't cover TikTok's like/comment buttons or the caption.
- **Checking is manual.** Checking every claim automatically would make it feel more "active", but each check costs a web search and a few seconds. Having the user click to start keeps costs predictable. Automatically checking only the claims judged high-harm is a reasonable middle ground for later.
- **I left out a single score for the whole video**, on purpose, for the reason I gave earlier.

There's no "Supported" example in the mockup, but supported claims would get a green tag.

What would you change? In particular, does checking with a click feel active enough, or do you want claims checked automatically?

content.text:
Here's what changed:

- **When nothing's checkable, nothing shows.** Most videos are like that, so most of the time the extension is invisible.
- **When there are claims, you get a 26px dot with a number in it.** It's dark and see-through, sits in the corner away from TikTok's buttons and caption, and is about the size of the like icon.
- **Hovering shows one line of text**, so you know what the number means without opening anything.
- **Clicking opens a small 200px popover** with each claim on one line and a colored dot for its verdict. The ✕ or clicking away closes it.
- **The badge stays neutral after checking.** The verdict colors are only inside the popover, so the video never gets a red warning label on it. I chose this because a red dot would draw attention to the video before you've decided to look. If you'd rather see that something's wrong without opening it, a contradicted claim could turn the dot red.

Two more ideas I didn't build:

- **Pause the video when the popover opens** and resume when it closes, so you don't miss anything while reading.
- **Let users turn off the dot** and only check videos when they press a keyboard shortcut. That could suit people who want no overlay at all.

Is this small enough? And should the dot turn red when a claim is contradicted, or stay neutral?

**The original rollout (May 2024)**
- TikTok partnered with the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) and became the first media-sharing platform to implement its Content Credentials technology.
- The system works by reading metadata. Content Credentials attaches metadata to content that the platform can use to instantly recognize and label AIGC.
- It started with images and videos. The feature has started rolling out but currently only applies to images and videos. TikTok plans to expand the tool to audio-only content soon.
- TikTok's existing labeling still applies alongside it. TikTok has already been requiring that content creators label realistic AIGC for over a year, along with anything made with its own TikTok AI effects.

- The credentials survive downloads. "Over the coming months, we'll also start attaching Content Credentials to TikTok content, which will remain on content when downloaded," the release explains. - Because of this, a re-upload from elsewhere can still be flagged. Content Credentials will remain attached to TikToks even if they're downloaded, meaning the content can be marked as AI-generated if it's later reuploaded to the platform.

The post also says C2PA shipped version 2.3 in February 2026.

Web search results for query: "AI generated video detection API accuracy Sora Veo detector false positives 2026"

Links: [{"title":"EA-Swin: An Embedding-Agnostic Swin Transformer for AI-Generated Video Detection","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.17260"},{"title":"AI & Agents","url":"https://fast.io/resources/ai-video-detector-tools-2026/"},{"title":"chatgpt fails to spot 92 of fake videos made by openais own sora tool","url":"https://the-decoder.com/chatgpt-fails-to-spot-92-of-fake-videos-made-by-openais-own-sora-tool/"},{"title":"the decoder","url":"https://the-decoder.com/?p=31375"},{"title":"2025 2026%2C%20Media Steffen%20Kuenn","url":"https://excellence-edlab.maastrichtuniversity.nl/sites/excellenceedlab/files/2026-05/2025-2026%2C%20Media-Steffen%20Kuenn.pdf"},{"title":"jaswin hargun","url":"https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~lindell/teaching/2529/past_projects/2025/report/jaswin-hargun.pdf"},{"title":"AI Video Detector Tools Tested: Why Detection Keeps Failing in 2026","url":"https://popularaitools.ai/blog/ai-video-detector/"},{"title":"AI Video Detector API","url":"https://detection.aiornot.com/ai-video-detector-api"},{"title":"how to spot fake ai videos created by openais sora 2","url":"https://macmyths.com/how-to-spot-fake-ai-videos-created-by-openais-sora-2/"}]

I found no independent, published false-positive rates for commercial AI video detection APIs against Sora or Veo. The best evidence is an academic study showing high false positives for research detectors, plus a few press tests and vendor claims that don't settle the question.

**Academic benchmarks.** A University of Toronto student project built a Sora 2 dataset and tested three research detectors. It reported consistently high false positive rates and a lack of clear decision boundaries, especially for videos with rapid transitions or stylized content. It is a student report, so treat it as directional rather than definitive. A separate 2026 paper notes that Veo and Sora in mid-2024, followed by newer generations, has significantly narrowed the perceptual gap between real and synthetic videos, which makes detection harder over time.

**Commercial tools.** A 2026 review says that for Hive Moderation, BitMind, and UncoVAI, none publish an accuracy figure, none publish a false-positive rate, and Sora 2 outputs after light mastering routinely slip past all three. Hive's API is described as multi-modal, and what's missing: an accuracy figure, a false-positive rate, processing speed, batch throughput, or any independent benchmark. That review is a blog, so its claims are secondhand. AI or Not's API page advertises 98.9% AI Detection Accuracy, but that figure is based on image datasets, not video. Another roundup relies on self-reported accuracy on datasets like FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF, and proprietary test sets, which is vendor-supplied.

**Chatbot and human tests.** NewsGuard tested 20 Sora videos with three chatbots. xAI's Grok failed to identify 95 percent of test videos as AI-generated. OpenAI's ChatGPT had an error rate of 92.5 percent, while Google's Gemini performed best at 78 percent. These are false negatives on general-purpose assistants, not purpose-built detectors. A 2025 survey of human viewers found 52.4% overall accuracy at spotting AI video from Veo and Sora, close to chance.

**Provenance caveats.** Visual inspection is unreliable. One guide says appearance alone cannot reliably identify whether a video was created by Sora 2 or by another generator, or whether ordinary editing caused the apparent anomaly. It also notes that OpenAI's safety article dated March 23, 2026 states that the consumer Sora product was no longer available as of April 26, 2026.

**Bottom line:** For an evaluation, ask vendors for false-positive rates on recent Sora and Veo outputs, especially after re-encoding, cropping, or audio removal, and test on your own labeled sample. Also check whether real footage with stylization or fast cuts gets flagged, since that is where the academic work found the weakest results.
